elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 登革热出血热仍然是印度尼西亚的重要公共卫生问题,YouTube已成为健康信息传播的主要渠道。识别有影响力的人物对于公共卫生传播至关重要,但现有的社交网络分析主要依赖文本,忽略了诸如视频缩略图等视觉信号。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究提出了一种基于自适应门控融合的多模态框架,结合文本和视觉特征,而不使用任何音频模态。通过IndoBERT提取文本特征,通过ResNet-50提取视觉特征,并在每个维度上自适应融合,每个通道上进行聚合,构建了一个基于内容的共受众网络,并使用PageRank进行分析。
elements_zh.methods: Using 33,233 Indonesian comments from 5,365 videos across 1,129 collected channels (1,084 retained after language filtering) over 2021 to 2025, an ablation study with stratified five-fold cross-validation shows the fused representation reaches 79.52 percent accuracy and 78.42 percent macro F1, outperforming text and visual baselines.
elements_zh.main_results: KOMPASTV、Kata Dokter和Halodoc被认定为最具影响力的角色。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,他们的框架通过整合文本和视觉特征,能够有效识别YouTube上登革热出血热信息传播中的有影响力角色,这与现有仅依赖文本的方法相比是一种新颖的途径。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为在社交媒体平台如YouTube上监测和管理登革热出血热信息的公共卫生策略提供信息,有助于更有效地针对有影响力的角色进行健康传播。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于印尼的YouTube数据,并依赖于用户评论,这可能无法完全代表更广泛的讨论。由于研究集中在单一平台和区域,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Clinical and Laboratory Profile of Dengue Cases in a Tertiary Care Hospital, Dhaka
papers.abstract: Background: Dengue fever is a painful, rapidly spreading vector-borne viral disease of global public health concern. The most recent dengue outbreaks in Bangladesh have demonstrated epidemiological patterns distinctly different from previous ones, with notable shifts in clinical presentation, serotype distribution, and disease severity.The aim of the study was to assess the clinical profile and laboratory findings of dengue patients presenting to a tertiary care hospital in Konia, Gazipur City, Dhaka. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted in the Department of Medicine, Tairunnessa Memorial Medical College & Hospital, Dhaka, Bangladesh, from February to December 2025. A total of 100 dengue patients were enrolled by purposive sampling. Diagnosis was established on the basis of clinical and laboratory parameters. Ethical approval was obtained and written informed consent was secured from all participants. Complete blood count, liver function tests, renal function tests, NS1 antigen, and dengue IgM/IgG serology were performed. Platelet count, haemoglobin, and haematocrit were monitored serially. Data were expressed as mean ± SD, frequency, and percentage. Chi-square and Z-proportion tests were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, Version 26.0. A p-value 1 was observed in 65% of patients versus

papers.title: Retinal Vascular Complications of Dengue Fever, an Unexplored Entity:
papers.abstract: Introduction: Systemic manifestations of dengue fever are well characterised, however ocular involvement has historically been considered a rare and under-recognised complication. Although less common,it can lead to visual impairment or blindness if not promptly addressed. Case Report: We describe a case series of five patients, all with clinically and serologically confirmed dengue fever who developed retinal vascular complications. Demographic data were extracted, along with systemic history (interval between dengue infection diagnosis to the onset of ocular symptoms, and interval between visual complaint to ophthalmic evaluation), and presenting best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). Pre-existing identifiable causes of retinal vascular occlusion (RVO) , if any, were recorded. All patients underwent fundus photo and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) examinations. Discussion: Seven eyes of five patients were included, all patients were female with a mean age of 25.8 years (range 19-32 years). None had identifiable pre-existing risk factor for RVO. The mean interval between dengue fever diagnosis to the onset of visual symptoms was 9.6 days (range 7-14 days). Patient one presented with sequential, bilateral central retinal artery occlusion; patient two came in with bilateral Purtscher-like retinopathy. Another patients exhibit paracentral acute-middle maculopathy (PAMM), and branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). Presenting BCVA ranged widely from 20/20 with paracentral scotoma to 20/800, reflecting the heterogenous severity of the vascular insult across the cohort. Conclusion: Dengue fever can produce a diverse spectrum of retinal vascular complications, typically manifesting one to three weeks after the onset of systemic illness. Spectral-domain OCT is central to the diagnosis, even when clinical examination is unremarkable. Prompt recognition and management is needed to avoid ocular complications and visual impairment. Keywords: dengue fever, dengue eye disease, retinal vascular occlusion, macular edema

analysis.summary_en: This case report explores the under-recognised retinal vascular complications of dengue fever, highlighting a diverse spectrum of ocular manifestations typically occurring one to three weeks after systemic illness onset. Five patients with confirmed dengue fever developed retinal vascular issues, including central retinal artery occlusion, Purtscher-like retinopathy, paracentral acute-middle maculopathy (PAMM), and branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). The mean interval between dengue diagnosis and visual symptoms was 9.6 days. Spectral-domain OCT is emphasized as a critical diagnostic tool, even when clinical findings are inconspicuous. The study underscores the importance of early detection and management to prevent visual impairment. However, the evidence is limited to a single case series, which may not fully represent the broader population or long-term outcomes.

papers.title_zh: 登革热致视网膜血管并发症:一种未被探索的实体的视网膜血管并发症:
papers.source_body_en: Introduction: Systemic manifestations of dengue fever are well characterised, however ocular involvement has historically been considered a rare and under-recognised complication. Although less common,it can lead to visual impairment or blindness if not promptly addressed. Case Report: We describe a case series of five patients, all with clinically and serologically confirmed dengue fever who developed retinal vascular complications. Demographic data were extracted, along with systemic history (interval between dengue infection diagnosis to the onset of ocular symptoms, and interval between visual complaint to ophthalmic evaluation), and presenting best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). Pre-existing identifiable causes of retinal vascular occlusion (RVO) , if any, were recorded. All patients underwent fundus photo and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) examinations. Discussion: Seven eyes of five patients were included, all patients were female with a mean age of 25.8 years (range 19-32 years). None had identifiable pre-existing risk factor for RVO. The mean interval between dengue fever diagnosis to the onset of visual symptoms was 9.6 days (range 7-14 days). Patient one presented with sequential, bilateral central retinal artery occlusion; patient two came in with bilateral Purtscher-like retinopathy. Another patients exhibit paracentral acute-middle maculopathy (PAMM), and branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). Presenting BCVA ranged widely from 20/20 with paracentral scotoma to 20/800, reflecting the heterogenous severity of the vascular insult across the cohort. Conclusion: Dengue fever can produce a diverse spectrum of retinal vascular complications, typically manifesting one to three weeks after the onset of systemic illness. Spectral-domain OCT is central to the diagnosis, even when clinical examination is unremarkable. Prompt recognition and management is needed to avoid ocular complications and visual impairment. Keywords: dengue fever, dengue eye disease, retinal vascular occlusion, macular edema
papers.abstract_zh: 引言:登革热的系统表现已被充分描述,但眼部受累历来被认为是一种罕见且未被充分认识的并发症。尽管较为少见,但若不及时处理,可能导致视力损害或失明。病例报告:我们描述了五例患者的病例系列,这些患者均经临床和血清学确诊为登革热,并出现了视网膜血管并发症。收集了人口统计数据、系统病史(从登革病毒感染诊断到眼部症状发作的时间间隔,以及从视力问题出现到眼科评估的时间间隔),以及初始最佳矫正视力(BCVA)。记录了所有患者是否存在已知的视网膜血管阻塞(RVO)的可识别原因。所有患者均接受了眼底照相和光谱域光学相干断层扫描(SD-OCT)检查。讨论:纳入了五名患者的七只眼睛,所有患者均为女性,平均年龄为25.8岁(年龄范围19-32岁)。无患者存在可识别的RVO风险因素。从登革热感染诊断到视力症状发作的平均时间间隔为9.6天(范围7-14天)。患者一表现为双侧中央动脉阻塞;患者二在就诊时出现双侧Purtscher样视网膜病变。其他患者则表现出旁中心性急性中期黄斑病变(PAMM)和分支视网膜静脉阻塞(BRVO)。初始BCVA范围广泛,从伴有旁中心暗点的20/20到20/800,反映了队列研究中血管损伤的异质性严重程度。结论:登革热可导致多种视网膜血管并发症,通常在系统性疾病发作后1至3周出现。即使临床检查无明显异常,光谱域OCT在诊断诊断中也至关重要。及时识别和管理是避免眼部并发症和视力损害的关键。关键词:登革热,登革热眼病,视网膜血管阻塞,黄斑水肿

papers.title: Meteorological predictors of dengue hemorrhagic fever incidence in Cilacap Regency, Indonesia: A time series analysis
papers.abstract: Objective: To analyze the nonlinear relationship between meteorological predictors and dengue hemorrhagic fever, and to quantify the meteorologically attributable fraction of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) during 2021-2025 in Cilacap Regency. Methods: This ecological time series design used sequential three-stage analytical tools, including a cross-correlation function (CCF) analysis applied to identify lag structures, Granger causality within a vector autoregression (VAR) framework used to confirm directional temporal precedence, and a quasi-Poisson Distributed Lag Nonlinear Model (DLNM) with natural cubic spline crossbases over a 28-day lag window used to estimate the exposure-response relationship. Autoregressive terms alongside long-term trends and seasonal splines were incorporated to account for autocorrelation and potential confounding. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在分析气象预测因子与登革出血热(DHF)发病率 之间的非线性关系,并量化 2021-2025 年期间印度尼西亚 cilacap 县 DHF 的气象归因分数。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究采用生态时间序列设计,分析了 2021 年至 2025 年期间印度尼西亚 cilacap 县的数据。研究包括连续的三阶段分析工具,以评估 DHF 与气象预测因子之间的关系。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究采用交叉相关函数(CCF)分析以识别滞后结构,使用 媒介 自回归(VAR)框架内的格兰杰因果关系检验以确认时间顺序的单向性,并采用准泊松分布滞后非线性模型(DLNM)以估计暴露-反应关系,该模型在 28 天的滞后窗口内使用自然三次样条交叉基底。
elements_zh.main_results: 格兰杰因果关系检验确认了 DHF 与所有四个预测因子之间的单向关系,包括平均温度、降雨量、相对湿度和风速(所有 P < 0.05)。每日降雨量是主要预测因子,其相对风险(RR)为 4.23(95% CI 2.10-8.52),归因分数为 27.58%。平均温度表现出 J 型暴露-反应曲线,其保护性最低点为 26.5°C,且在高于 28°C 时风险显著升高(RR 2.13;95% CI 1.43-3.19;AF = 6.22%)。相对湿度(AF = -14.40%)和风速(AF = -3.37%)表现出复杂的非线性模式,贡献了净保护性归因分数。总体而言,该模型解释了 52.26% 的零偏差(QAIC = 3984.23)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究发现,降雨量和温度是与 cilacap 县 DHF 发病率 最强相关的气象预测因子,突显了这些因素与 DHF 之间的非线性关系。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,将气象预测因子纳入 媒介 控制计划和早期预警系统,有助于预防 cilacap 县 DHF 暴发。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究中纳入了自回归项和长期趋势,以考虑自相关性和潜在的混杂因素,但研究的生态设计可能限制了推断个体层面因果关系的能力。证据强度中等,因为其基于摘要分析。

news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Fiji + 17 more Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 18 September 2026) Format Situation Report Sources SPC WHO Posted 18 Sep 2026 Originally published 18 Sep 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 732.62 KB) HIGHLIGHTS • Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs). • During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Naoero, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Naoero (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1). • Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 721 dengue confirmed cases, 173 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific. • The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 9 754 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year. • In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu. • The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases. • Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation. • The Cook Islands officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 25 May 2026. • Tonga has officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 31 July 2026. • As of 7 August 2026: o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate. o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna. elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 截至2026年9月18日,太平洋地区共记录了21,258例确诊病例和21例死亡病例。死亡病例分别出现在斐济(8例)、萨摩亚(7例)、汤加(3例)、瑙鲁(2例)和基里巴斯(1例)。太平洋综合征监测系统(PSSS)至今已报告了9,754例登革热样疾病(DLI)病例,与去年同期相比呈现下降趋势。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 多个太平洋岛国和领地(PICs)已正式宣布登革热暴发,而瓦努阿图谢法省的暴发仍在持续。库克群岛和汤加已正式宣布结束其登革热暴发。太平洋综合征监测系统(PSSS)继续监测DLI病例,疫情情况正在被持续跟踪。

news.title_zh: 太平洋地区的登革热:多国疫情状况(截至2026年9月18日) - ReliefWeb
news.source_body_en: As of 18 September 2026, dengue outbreaks have been reported across twelve Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs) since 1 January 2025. The most affected regions include American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia, which account for 94% of confirmed cases. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific, with fatalities reported in Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Naoero, and Kiribati. The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) reported 9,754 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases, showing a lower trend than the same period last year. Outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga, and Shefa province, Vanuatu, with the latter still experiencing ongoing transmission of DENV-1. The Cook Islands and Tonga have since declared the end of their outbreaks, while low levels of transmission are observed in several other countries.
news.content_zh: 截至2026年9月18日,自2025年1月1日起,登革热暴发已在十二个太平洋岛国和领地(PICs)中被报告。受影响最严重的地区包括美属萨摩亚、库克群岛、萨摩亚和新喀里多尼亚,这些地区占确诊病例的94%。在太平洋地区共记录了21,258例确诊病例和21例死亡病例,其中斐济、萨摩亚、汤加、瑙鲁和基里巴斯均报告了死亡病例。太平洋综合征监测系统(PSSS)报告了9,754例登革热样疾病(DLI)病例,显示出比去年同期更低的趋势。登革热暴发在新喀里多尼亚、汤加和瓦努阿图的谢法省被正式宣布,而后者仍持续存在DENV-1的传播。库克群岛和汤加已宣布结束其登革热暴发,而在其他几个国家仍观察到低水平的传播。

news.excerpt: Floridians should be concerned, but not panicking, over cases of dengue fever spiraling up. There are things you can do to stay safe.

news.content_title: How worried should Florida residents, visitors be about dengue?
news.content: Should Florida residents and visitors be concerned about the surge of dengue cases in the state? Yes, but don't panic. There are things you can do to help prevent being bitten by the mosquitoes carrying the virus. As of Sept. 12, there have been 152 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in the state, including one death. Compare that to 62 cases in all of 2025, and it's fast approaching the highest number in recent memory: 199 cases reported in 2023 . Dengue — sometimes called breakbone fever because of the pain it sometimes brings — is caused by the bite of a mosquito carrying the virus. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal About 1 in 20 patients with dengue develop severe, life-threatening disease called severe dengue, according to the Centers for Disease Control, and because there are four types of dengue viruses, people can be infected several times in their life. Here's what you should know about dengue in Florida and suggestions on what you can do to stay safe, especially if you live in the state's dengue hotspot on the state's West Coast. As of Sept. 12, there have been 152 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported, an increase of 41 new locally acquired case in one week, nearly all of them in Hillsborough County, according to the Sept. 12 update from the Florida Department of Health . Hillsborough County continues to lead the state with 134 confirmed cases, while the remaining cases are scattered around Miami-Dade, Pinellas, Pasco, Orange, and Palm Beach counties. Eleven counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Florida is facing one of its worst outbreaks of the mosquito-borne illness in decades, according to Ophthalmology Advisor. The worst year in recent records was 2023, when 199 cases were reported by the Florida Department of Health. As of Sept. 12, there were 152 locally acquired cases of dengue in Florida. "Dengue is the most common vector-borne viral disease in the world, causing an estimated 50 million to 100 million infections and 25,000 deaths each year," according to the Centers for Disease Control. From 1946 to 1980, no cases of dengue acquired in the continental United States had been reported, the CDC said. Then a New York physician in 2009 treated a woman with dengue who had visited Key West . Two other dengue infections were confirmed in Key West residents the CDC said. Since that time, outbreaks and sporadic local dengue cases have been reported. Florida cases of locally acquired dengue by year based on numbers provided by Florida Department of Health: There were 90 cases of dengue in Key West between 2009 and 2010, and 23 cases in Martin County in 2013 , according to the National Library of Medicine. There were early reports of dengue in the Florida from the Dry Tortugas that date back to 1903, and in Miami in 1904 and 1908, according to the National Library of Medicine. "More widespread outbreaks that affected close to 12,000 people occurred in 1905 and included Key West, Miami, Tampa, Jacksonville, and probably other locations. "Outbreaks were reported from Hillsborough — the hotspot in the 2026 outbreak — and Monroe counties in 1907. "In 1921-1922, the widespread dengue outbreak that affected Texas, Louisiana, Georgia, and Florida resulted in almost 83,000 cases and 69 deaths," according to the National Library of Medicine. "In 1934, another dengue epidemic affected a large portion of the state including Miami, Tampa and numerous other cities and populated areas and produced more than 1,600 reported cases. "At the time, it was estimated that more than 10% of the population of Dade County and that as many as 15,000 people in the city of Miami — which had a population of 135,000 — were infected with the virus." Yes, but there are precautions you can take. Just before Labor Day, Florida State Surgeon General Dr. Joseph A. Ladapo urged Florida residents to take a "few simple steps to protect themselves and their families from mosquito bites": Remove standing water around your home. "Mosquitoes do not need a large amount of water to reproduce. Even a bottle cap of standing water can be enough for mosquitoes to breed," according to the Florida Department of Health. "Individual prevention helps protect you and your community," Ladapo said. " Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname "breakbone fever") Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue is sometimes called " breakbone fever " because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman who is infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight or premature birth. "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body's immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don't accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties as of Sept. 12: A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Cheryl McCloud is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. You can get all of Florida's best content directly in your inbox each weekday day by signing up for the free newsletter, Florida TODAY, at https://heraldtribune.com/newsletters. news.content: CubaHeadlines Dengue Cases in Cuba Surge Dramatically in 2026, October Expected to Hit Peak Tuesday, September 22, 2026 by Felix Ortiz Discover more Public Health Health Conditions Infectious Diseases Aedes aegypti mosquito - Image by © isglobal.org The island of Cuba has recorded 7,133 cases of dengue in the year 2026, a figure that significantly surpasses the typical levels for this period, according to the latest data from the Global Dengue Observatory (GDO) at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. Miaminews coverage Discover more Biological Sciences Medical Literature & Resources Health Foundations & Medical Research Relying on official data and statistical models to predict the progression of the disease, the observatory reports that the current season's cases are at an elevated level. The number of reported and estimated cases is roughly 7.4 times higher than what historical trends in the country would predict. "So far in 2026, the reported cases have dramatically exceeded expectations. The numbers are currently on the rise, aligning with the seasonal trends observed in previous years," the GDO highlighted in their analysis. Summer Surge in Dengue Cases August saw the most significant increase, with an estimated 3,214 cases—far exceeding what's typically expected at this time of year. In July, the estimate was around 2,173 cases. The GDO clarifies that official data are only available through June, with subsequent figures being estimates to address the usual delays in epidemiological reporting. Expected Peak and Multiple Viral Strains The situation could deteriorate in the upcoming weeks. Historically, October is known to be the peak month for dengue transmission in Cuba, indicating that the country may not have reached the season's climax yet. Miaminews coverage The surge in cases comes after an alert by the Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) in June regarding the risk of a dengue epidemic. At that time, the Vice Minister of Public Health, Carilda Peña, warned that all four serotypes of the virus—DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4—are circulating simultaneously in the country. The presence of multiple serotypes raises the risk of complications, particularly for individuals who have had dengue before and might now be infected with a different variant. Hotspots and Health Alerts Currently, the provinces of Guantánamo, Villa Clara, and Matanzas are experiencing the highest transmission rates. As of September 9, the municipalities of Imías, Baracoa, and Guantánamo city reported active transmission, with over 30 confirmed PCR cases and circulation of serotypes 2, 3, and 4. This week, the municipality of Manuel Tames in Guantánamo was put on high alert due to the rising dengue cases. In Villa Clara, the municipality of Ranchuelo saw a spike in dengue hemorrhagic fever cases in July, with at least 12 individuals hospitalized during the outbreak. Environmental and Social Factors Discover more Insects & Entomology Executive Branch Cuban migration resources The spread of dengue is occurring amidst conditions that facilitate the breeding of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary vector of the virus. Accumulated garbage, water leaks, and the need to store water during frequent power outages are factors cited by experts and health authorities as complicating efforts to control the vector. This recent surge follows a 2025 marked by rampant arbovirus activity in Cuba, where MINSAP reported over 81,900 combined cases of dengue and chikungunya, acknowledging at least 55 deaths. Miaminews coverage Frequently Asked Questions about Dengue in Cuba Why are dengue cases increasing in Cuba? Dengue cases are rising due to the simultaneous circulation of all four virus serotypes, environmental conditions that favor mosquito breeding, and delays in epidemiological reporting. What measures are being taken to control dengue in Cuba? Efforts include alerting the public, monitoring transmission hotspots, and addressing environmental factors like garbage and water storage that facilitate mosquito breeding. What are the risks of having multiple dengue serotypes circulating? Having multiple serotypes increases the risk of severe complications, especially in individuals previously infected with a different serotype, as they may develop more severe forms of the disease. analysis_en.time: The surge in dengue cases in Cuba is reported to have occurred in 2026, with the latest data as of September 22, 2026, and the expected peak in October. The GDO's analysis was conducted as of September 9, and the current rise is noted as of September 23, 2026.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The outbreak is primarily affecting the provinces of Guantánamo, Villa Clara, and Matanzas in Cuba. The entire country is impacted, with the Global Dengue Observatory (GDO) providing national-level data and analysis.
analysis_en.event: Cuba has experienced a dramatic surge in dengue cases in 2026, with 7,133 cases reported as of September 22, 2026. The GDO at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine reported that the number of cases is roughly 7.4 times higher than historical trends. The Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) issued an alert in June regarding the risk of an epidemic.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: As of September 22, 2026, Cuba has recorded 7,133 dengue cases, with an estimated 3,214 cases in August and 2,173 in July. The GDO notes that the current season's cases are at an elevated level. The presence of all four serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4) increases the risk of severe complications, particularly for individuals previously infected with a different serotype. The GDO also mentions that the situation could deteriorate in the upcoming weeks.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The GDO clarifies that official data are only available through June, with subsequent figures being estimates. The Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) has been monitoring the outbreak, issuing alerts, and addressing environmental factors that contribute to mosquito breeding. The GDO's analysis is based on official data and statistical models, and the current rise in cases is noted as aligning with seasonal trends.

news.title_zh: 2026年古巴登革热病例激增,10月预计达到高峰 - 古巴头条
news.source_body_en: In 2026, Cuba has seen a dramatic surge in dengue cases, with 7,133 reported as of September 22, significantly exceeding historical trends. The Global Dengue Observatory (GDO) at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine noted that the current season's cases are roughly 7.4 times higher than expected. The Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) issued an alert in June, warning of an epidemic risk, and confirmed that all four dengue serotypes—DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4—are circulating simultaneously. This situation is particularly concerning as it increases the risk of severe complications, especially for individuals previously infected with a different serotype. The provinces of Guantánamo, Villa Clara, and Matanzas are experiencing the highest transmission rates. The GDO's analysis relies on official data and statistical models, with estimates used for months after June due to delays in reporting. The outbreak is expected to peak in October, aligning with historical seasonal trends. Efforts to control the outbreak include public alerts, monitoring hotspots, and addressing environmental factors that facilitate mosquito breeding.

The death comes amid one of Florida's most significant dengue outbreaks in recent years and as health officials monitor rising case numbers in several U.S. jurisdictions. A spokesperson for the Florida Department of Health told Newsweek that they remain focused on "protecting Florida’s communities through ongoing prevention and response efforts," adding that they are sharing prevention messaging through social media, local media and community partners. What Is Dengue Fever? Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral illness that usually causes flu-like symptoms including fever, headache and severe joint pain. It is not generally fatal, but in rare cases can progress to life-threatening complications such as shock, internal bleeding and organ failure. Dengue Fever in the US The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says the risk of widespread dengue transmission in the continental United States remains low, and most cases are as a result of people coming back from other countries with higher levels of dengue. Of the 1,927 dengue cases reported in U.S. states and territories this year, Puerto Rico has recorded 907 and American Samoa 437, according to CDC data. Florida's 332 reported cases are the highest among U.S. states. State health officials have also reported more than 150 locally acquired infections this year, meaning residents were infected within Florida rather than during travel abroad. While dengue has reappeared periodically in Florida since 2009, Kristi Miley, a professor in the Global Health Infectious Disease Research Center at the University of South Florida, told Newsweek that the current pattern appears to reflect a concentrated outbreak in the Tampa Bay area rather than a statewide surge. "The Bay Area has seen more locally acquired cases than in previous years, indicating a localized outbreak in Hillsborough County's mosquito population rather than a statewide increase," she said. What Are the Symptoms of Dengue Fever? Dengue symptoms usually begin two to seven days after being bitten by an infected mosquito and commonly include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle pain, nausea and vomiting and rash, according to the CDC. Around one in four people infected with dengue will become sick, and most will recover within a week. Though experts say older adults, young children and people who are immunocompromised face a greater risk of developing severe disease. Dengue can also be more severe in people who have previously been infected with a different strain of the virus. Signs of severe dengue fever include severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool and extreme fatigue. "Many people may not seek care and fully recover without incidence; however it can be life-threatening for some," Miley said. How Unusual Is the Dengue Outbreak? The outbreak is unusual for the Tampa Bay region. Miley explained that Hillsborough County "has not recorded this level of dengue infection since the 1930s." Recent outbreaks in Florida have been largely linked to recent warm weather. Health officials say warm temperatures and rainfall can increase mosquito populations and create conditions that allow outbreaks to occur. Miley explained that Florida's rainy season creates ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, which spread dengue. The insects can reproduce in very small amounts of standing water and are considered "day-biters," increasing exposure risk for people who spend time outdoors. Hillsborough County authorities have increased mosquito-control efforts during the outbreak, including spraying and monitoring mosquito populations. "The Department also continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas," the Florida Department of Health said. "These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." Officials have said recent surveillance suggests transmission may be slowing, although residents are still being urged to take precautions against mosquito bites. news.summary_zh: Newsweek reports that Florida has recorded its first dengue fever death of 2026, with an 80-year-old woman from Hillsborough County succumbing to complications including septic shock and multiple organ failure. This death occurs amid one of Florida's most significant dengue outbreaks in recent years, with nearly 2,000 cases reported nationwide and 332 in Florida. The outbreak is concentrated in the Tampa Bay area, with over 150 locally acquired infections this year. Health officials are monitoring the situation and have increased mosquito-control efforts, including spraying and monitoring, to reduce populations and limit disease transmission. The Florida Department of Health emphasizes ongoing prevention and response efforts, urging residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. While the CDC notes that widespread dengue transmission in the continental U.S. remains low, most cases are linked to travel from countries with higher dengue prevalence. The outbreak is unusual for the Tampa Bay region, with Hillsborough County experiencing this level of infection since the 1930s. Officials suggest that warm weather and rainfall have contributed to the mosquito population growth, creating ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, which are known to spread dengue. The situation remains under active investigation and monitoring.

OffOn Stream on What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports 1st death and cases rise Florida has confirmed 152 locally acquired cases of dengue this year. What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports 1st death and cases rise Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images ByMary Kekatos September 21, 2026, 7:05 PM Share The Florida Department of Health confirmed the state's first death from dengue fever this year as cases of the mosquito-borne illness continue to rise. The department did not provide any details about the patient including name, age, sex or residence. The Tampa Bay Times, which first reported the death, described the patient as an 80-year-old Tampa woman who died on Sept. 4. "The Department has completed its epidemiological investigation and acknowledges the first dengue fever-related death in Hillsborough County. To protect the privacy of the individual, additional details and information regarding the case are confidential," a spokesperson for the FDOH told ABC News in a state,emt/ The FDOH did not immediately return ABC News' request for comment. Related Dengue fever cases rise to 6,800 in US amid 2 new infections in Los Angeles: CDC For the week ending Sept. 12, Florida has confirmed 152 locally acquired cases of dengue, according to data from the state health department. This is the highest number recorded since 2023, when the state saw 189 locally acquired cases over the course of the year, data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows. Hillsborough County -- which includes Tampa -- has reported the most cases so far this year with 134, according to the FDOH. Other counties with confirmed cases include Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco and Pinellas. Close-up of a mosquito biting human skin. Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images Dengue viruses are spread through bites from infected Aedes species mosquitoes, mostly found in tropical and subtropical regions, according to the CDC. These mosquitoes are also responsible for spreading Zika and chikungunya viruses. Dengue can be caused by dengue virus strains 1, 2, 3 or 4. A person also can be infected with dengue multiple times over the course of their life. About one in four people who contract dengue develop symptoms which typically last two to seven days and are usually mild. This may include fever, rash, nausea, vomiting, muscle pain, joint pain and bone pain. Popular Reads What GLP-1 users should know about the potential risk of a rare type of vision loss 2 days ago 2nd possible measles exposure reported in Philadelphia at airport Sep 21 A North Dakota man's murder conviction was overturned. He may now be deported Sep 21 About one in 20 infected people will develop severe dengue, which can lead to shock, internal bleeding and, in some cases, death, the CDC said. There are no disease-specific treatments for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, fluids and over-the-counter medications to relieve symptoms. Patients with severe illness often need to be hospitalized and receive additional supportive treatments, such as intravenous fluids. Related Puerto Rico declares public health emergency as dengue fever cases rise The CDC warns patients not to take aspirin or ibuprofen; it can trigger inflammation or bleeding of the stomach lining. Currently, there is no dengue vaccine available in the U.S. In 2021, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a vaccine for children between ages 9 and 16 who have a laboratory-confirmed previous dengue virus infection and live in areas where dengue is endemic, but it has since been discontinued. Methods to help prevent dengue infection include using effective mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeve shirts and long pants when outside and staying in places with air conditioning when possible. The CDC also recommends emptying containers of still or stagnant water to eliminate places where mosquitos can breed. ABC News' Youri Benadjaoud contributed to this report. elements_zh.time: 佛罗里达州卫生部确认,今年该州首次报告了登革热死亡病例,而该蚊媒疾病病例数仍在持续上升。《坦帕湾时报》首先报道了这一死亡病例,称患者是一名在9月去世的80岁坦帕女性。卫生部门未提供任何关于患者的额外信息,包括姓名、年龄、性别或住址。根据州卫生部的数据,CDC数据显示,截至9月12日当周,佛罗里达州已确认152例本地感染的登革热病例。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 佛罗里达州,特别是希尔斯伯勒县(包括坦帕),截至目前已报告最多的病例,共134例,根据佛罗里达州卫生部的数据。其他有确诊病例的县包括迈阿密-戴德县、橙县、棕榈滩县、帕斯科县和皮尼拉斯县。根据CDC的数据,登革病毒通过感染的Aedes物种蚊虫叮咬传播,这些蚊虫主要分布在热带和亚热带地区。
elements_zh.event: 登革热是一种由登革病毒毒株1、2、3或4引起的蚊媒疾病。一个人在其一生中可能会多次感染登革热。CDC建议休息、补充水分和使用非处方药物来缓解症状。重症患者通常需要住院并接受额外的支持性治疗,如静脉输液。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: As of the week ending Sept. This is the highest number recorded since 2023, when the state saw 189 locally acquired cases over the course of the year. The CDC warns that about one in four people who contract dengue develop symptoms, which typically last two to seven days and are usually mild. However, about one in 20 infected people will develop severe dengue, which can lead to shock, internal bleeding and, in some cases, death.
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 佛罗里达州卫生部已完成流行病学调查,并承认希尔斯伯勒县出现了首例与登革热相关的死亡病例。为保护个人隐私,关于该病例的更多细节和信息仍保持保密。CDC建议使用有效的驱蚊剂,外出时穿长袖衬衫和长裤,并尽可能待在有空调的环境中。此外,CDC还建议清除容器中的静水,以消除蚊虫繁殖的场所。

(Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images) (NEW YORK) — The Florida Department of Health confirmed the state’s first death from dengue fever this year as cases of the mosquito-borne illness continue to rise. The department did not provide any details about the patient including name, age, sex or residence. The Tampa Bay Times, which first reported the death, described the patient as an 80-year-old Tampa woman who died on Sept. 4. The FDOH did not immediately return ABC News’ request for comment. For the week ending Sept. 12, Florida has confirmed 152 locally acquired cases of dengue, according to data from the state health department. This is the highest number recorded since 2023, when the state saw 189 locally acquired cases over the course of the year, data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows. Hillsborough County — which includes Tampa — has reported the most cases so far this year with 134, according to the FDOH. Other counties with confirmed cases include Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco and Pinellas. Dengue viruses are spread through bites from infected Aedes species mosquitoes, mostly found in tropical and subtropical regions, according to the CDC. These mosquitoes are also responsible for spreading Zika and chikungunya viruses. Dengue can be caused by dengue virus strains 1, 2, 3 or 4. A person also can be infected with dengue multiple times over the course of their life. About one in four people who contract dengue develop symptoms which typically last two to seven days and are usually mild. This may include fever, rash, nausea, vomiting, muscle pain, joint pain and bone pain. About one in 20 infected people will develop severe dengue, which can lead to shock, internal bleeding and, in some cases, death, the CDC said. There are no disease-specific treatments for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, fluids and over-the-counter medications to relieve symptoms. Patients with severe illness often need to be hospitalized and receive additional supportive treatments, such as intravenous fluids. The CDC warns patients not to take aspirin or ibuprofen; it can trigger inflammation or bleeding of the stomach lining. Currently, there is no dengue vaccine available in the U.S. In 2021, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a vaccine for children between ages 9 and 16 who have a laboratory-confirmed previous dengue virus infection and live in areas where dengue is endemic, but it has since been discontinued. Methods to help prevent dengue infection include using effective mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeve shirts and long pants when outside and staying in places with air conditioning when possible. The CDC also recommends emptying containers of still or stagnant water to eliminate places where mosquitos can breed. ABC News’ Youri Benadjaoud contributed to this report. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Global editionWednesday, September 23, 2026 Streamline Search⌘KWriteSign inJoin Streamline StreamlineGlobal edition LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSportDirectoryHouse HuntingPeopleHistoryMore LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSport Back to News/Health Health Dr. Reddy's Secures Exclusive Indian Private Market Rights for Takeda's Qdenga Dengue Vaccine Dr. Reddy's Laboratories will distribute India's first approved dengue vaccine, Qdenga, in the private market starting in early 2027, following a collaboration with Japan's Takeda Pharmaceutical. Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Sep 18, 2026Updated Sep 18, 20264 min read Report article Follow on Google News Try askingWhy does this matter? Advertisement from Silva Gigiri. The first 10 seconds cannot be skipped. Ad playing Ad playing. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Dr. Reddy's Laboratories has entered an exclusive partnership with Japanese drugmaker Takeda Pharmaceutical Company to promote and distribute India's first approved dengue vaccine in the domestic private market. Under the agreement announced on Friday, September 18, 2026, the Hyderabad-based pharmaceutical company will handle the private distribution of the Qdenga vaccine for both paediatric and adult populations. The vaccine, which received marketing authorisation from India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026, is projected to become available in the first half of 2027. The collaboration represents a significant commercial and public health development in a country that has experienced an 11-fold increase in reported dengue cases over the past two decades. Financial terms of the distribution agreement remain confidential, but Takeda will retain full legal ownership of the vaccine, control over its manufacturing, and commercialisation rights for India's public procurement market. By securing exclusive private distribution rights, Dr. Reddy's bypasses standard price-capped therapeutic segments, capturing high-barrier retail vaccination flows in India's expanding urban healthcare markets. This move aligns with the company's broader strategy to pivot toward speciality pharmaceutical assets, complementing its existing portfolio of generic medicines. Following the announcement, shares of Dr. Reddy's Laboratories rose by up to 3 percent on the Bombay Stock Exchange, reaching an intraday high of ₹1,207.50. Regulatory Approval and Vaccine Mechanics The CDSCO cleared Qdenga—technically known as TAK-003—for individuals aged 4 to 60 years. Developed using recombinant DNA technology, the live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. Scientists built the vaccine on a weakened dengue virus type-2 (DENV-2) backbone, engineering it to include structural surface proteins from the DENV-1, DENV-3, and DENV-4 strains. This structural approach aims to provide broad immune coverage regardless of which specific serotype a patient encounters in the environment. Healthcare providers will administer the vaccine through subcutaneous injection in a two-dose regimen, spaced three months apart. Crucially, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended Qdenga for use in highly endemic countries without requiring pre-vaccination screening for prior dengue exposure. The absence of a pre-vaccination testing requirement streamlines administration in busy clinical settings, avoiding the delays and costs associated with serological screening. India's Dengue Burden and Serotype Circulation The introduction of a tetravalent vaccine addresses a complex epidemiological challenge in India. Dengue is an endemic mosquito-borne viral infection that causes severe flu-like illness, and in extreme cases, can progress to severe dengue accompanied by bleeding, organ impairment, and plasma leakage. Urbanisation, changing climate patterns, and increased domestic travel have expanded the geographical footprint of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary vector for the virus. Consequently, hospitals routinely face severe capacity constraints during the peak monsoon and post-monsoon transmission seasons. A recent nationwide molecular surveillance study conducted by the Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) illustrated the complexity of the local outbreak environment. The research confirmed that all four dengue serotypes are currently co-circulating across multiple regions of the country. Furthermore, the study found that one in 14 patients carried concurrent infections with multiple dengue serotypes. Because infection with one serotype does not confer long-term immunity against the others—and subsequent infections with different serotypes carry a higher risk of severe disease—a vaccine that addresses all four strains simultaneously is considered essential for effective population-level protection. Clinical Efficacy and Global Precedent Takeda has gathered substantial clinical data supporting the vaccine's efficacy through an extensive global clinical development programme involving more than 60,000 participants across endemic and non-endemic regions. According to a 2025 analysis released by Takeda, clinical trials demonstrated a 61.2 percent overall efficacy rate against virologically confirmed dengue. More importantly for public health systems, the vaccine showed an 84.1 percent efficacy rate in preventing dengue-related hospitalisations at a 4.5-year follow-up after vaccination. Since its initial regulatory clearances in 2022, Qdenga has secured approvals in more than 40 countries. The manufacturer reports that more than 32 million doses have already been distributed worldwide through various public and private immunisation programmes. The vaccine also holds a WHO prequalification, a designation that ensures the product meets stringent international standards for quality, safety, and efficacy. Public Health Integration and Future Milestones While the current agreement focuses exclusively on the private sector, both companies view the retail market launch as the first step in a broader deployment strategy. Regulatory processes, including price determination and the finalisation of local quality-assurance protocols, are ongoing. The precise pricing structure for the Indian market has not yet been announced, as the companies navigate the final administrative steps required before commercial distribution. Takeda executives have stated that securing a position in India's Universal Immunisation Programme remains a primary long-term objective. A recent recommendation by the Parliamentary Committee on Health to consider incorporating a dengue vaccine into the national programme suggests growing institutional support for public procurement. In the interim, Dr. Reddy's will leverage its extensive domestic distribution network to make the vaccine accessible to eligible patients who can afford private healthcare. The companies will jointly conduct disease awareness campaigns and engage with healthcare professionals to prepare for the 2027 rollout. Medical experts caution that while the vaccine provides a vital new tool, it must complement rather than replace existing vector control measures. Continued public health efforts to eliminate stagnant water and reduce mosquito populations remain necessary to comprehensively manage the disease burden in urban and rural communities alike. supplementary_news.content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Entertainment Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Motor Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Dengue in Cuba exceeds 7.4 times the expected level for 2026, and the peak typically occurs in October Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Tuesday, September 22, 2026 - 6:42 PM Mosquito Aedes aegyptiPhoto © isglobal.org Cuba has recorded 7,133 cases of dengue in 2026, a figure that greatly exceeds the usual levels for this time of year, according to updated data from the Global Dengue Observatory (GDO) at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. The observatory, which uses official data and statistical models to estimate the progression of the disease, places the current season at elevated levels and calculates that the reported and estimated cases so far represent approximately 7.4 times the expected level based on the country's historical behavior. "As of 2026, the reported cases far exceed the anticipated figures. Currently, the cases are on the rise, as expected for this time of year according to trends from previous years," stated the GDO in its analysis. August recorded the highest increase August recorded the highest monthly figure in recent months, with an estimated 3,214 cases, a number "far higher than what would typically be expected at this time of year." In July, the estimate had been 2,173 cases. The GDO clarifies that the official available data extends up to June, while the subsequent figures correspond to estimates made to adjust for the usual delays in epidemiological reporting. The situation could worsen in the coming weeks. According to historical patterns of dengue in Cuba, October tends to be the month with the highest transmission activity, meaning the country may not have reached the peak of the season yet. Graph showing the evolution of dengue cases in Cuba in 2026. Screenshot/Global Dengue Observatory. Four serotypes of the virus circulate on the island The increase in cases comes after the Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) warned in June about the risk of a dengue epidemic. The Deputy Minister of Public Health, Carilda Peña, then warned that all four serotypes of the virus are circulating simultaneously in Cuba: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. The presence of multiple serotypes increases the risk of complications, especially in individuals who have previously suffered from dengue and may become infected with a different variant of the virus. The main sources of transmission are currently concentrated in Guantánamo, Villa Clara, and Matanzas. As of September 9, the municipalities of Imías, Baracoa, and Guantánamo city were experiencing active transmission, with more than 30 confirmed cases by PCR and circulation of serotypes 2, 3, and 4. This week, the Guantanamo municipality of Manuel Tames was declared in a state of alarm due to the increase in dengue cases. In Villa Clara, the municipality of Ranchuelo reported an increase in patients with hemorrhagic dengue, with at least 12 individuals hospitalized during the outbreak. Trash, standing water, and power outages favor the mosquito The expansion of dengue occurs in a context marked by issues that favor the reproduction of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the main transmitter of the virus. The accumulation of garbage, water leaks, and the need to store it during power outages have been identified by specialists and health authorities as factors that complicate vector control. The current increase follows a 2025 marked by a strong circulation of arboviruses in Cuba. The MINSAP reported that that year more than 81,900 cases of dengue and chikungunya were recorded and acknowledged at least 55 fatalities. Neighboring States 23 sep 2026, 22:16 Ukraine Sets Temporary Residence Permit Rules for Foreign Contract Soldiers Florida Dengue Outbreak Sickens 134 People as Officials Confirm First Death Monday, 21 September 2026, 13:06 This 2006 photograph from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows a female Aedes aegypti mosquito feeding on blood from a human host. James Gathany/CDC/AP What once seemed limited to tropical travel is appearing closer to home, raising fresh concerns about mosquito-borne disease and climate change. Dengue, once associated mainly with tropical travel, is spreading into new regions. In Florida, an outbreak in Hillsborough County during the summer of 2026 affected 134 people. Based on data from CNN On September 18, the Florida Department of Health confirmed that the death of an elderly woman who died on September 4 was caused by dengue. This is the first confirmed fatality during the current outbreak. Back in August, local health officials warned of several cases acquired within the state. How dengue spreads The dengue virus does not spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. It is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, primarily the yellow fever mosquito, Aedes aegypti, which is widespread in Florida. They need only a small amount of standing water to breed and can bite throughout the day, not just at dawn or after sunset. A mosquito becomes infected after biting an infected person and can transmit the virus to someone else several days later. Approximately three-quarters of infected people develop no symptoms. In others, signs of illness usually appear 4–10 days after the bite. Dengue is also known as “breakbone fever” because of the severe pain it can cause in the muscles, joints, and bones. Typical symptoms include: a sudden high fever, severe headache and pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, and a blotchy rash. There are four types of dengue virus. A previous infection usually provides long-lasting protection against only one of them. A second infection with a different type can increase the risk of severe illness. Why severe dengue is dangerous Most patients recover in about a week. However, approximately one in 20 patients develops severe dengue, often just as the fever begins to subside – on the third to seventh day of illness. Fluid leaking from small blood vessels can lead to a sharp drop in blood pressure, bleeding, and organ damage. Those at greatest risk include infants, pregnant women, people over 65, and patients with diabetes, obesity, or kidney disease. Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme drowsiness or restlessness. Without treatment, severe dengue can be fatal for approximately 10% of patients. With timely hospitalization, that figure falls to less than 1%. There is no specific antiviral drug for dengue, so treatment involves controlling the fever, restoring fluid levels, and monitoring the patient’s condition. Aspirin, ibuprofen, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can increase the risk of bleeding. Dengue is spreading beyond the tropics According to the World Health Organization, more than 14 million cases of dengue were reported worldwide in 2024 across approximately 100 countries. That is a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases recorded in 2000. Rising temperatures, rapid urban growth, and international travel are contributing to the spread of the virus. In the United States, most cases are still linked to infections acquired abroad. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such cases in 2023 alone. However, in warm states, infected travelers can initiate local chains of transmission because mosquito vectors already live there. Of the 50 U.S. states, Florida faces the highest risk. More than 300 locally acquired cases were reported in Miami-Dade County between 2010 and 2024. Local transmission has also been recorded in Texas, California, Arizona, and Hawaii. A dengue vaccine exists, but it is used only in certain situations, including for children who live in areas with high levels of virus transmission and have previously had dengue. Therefore, reducing the risk depends primarily on protecting against mosquito bites and seeking medical care promptly if symptoms appear. Jeffrey Epstein Estate Shrinks to $107.6 Million as Victims Pursue New Lawsuits Monday, 21 September 2026, 13:05 Illustration created by Leah Abucayan/CNN/Getty A shrinking estate, disputed investments and a long list of beneficiaries are creating a high-stakes race over what remains. After Jeffrey Epstein’s death, the value of his estate fell from approximately $655.1 million to $107.6 million in assets. A new lawsuit brought by survivors could prolong the legal proceedings for several more years and affect payments to his closest advisers – attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn. As highlighted by CNN For a long time, survivors have accused Indyke and Kahn of providing Epstein with the financial and legal tools that enabled his activities and the sexual exploitation of hundreds of young women. In a lawsuit filed in August, they were described as key participants in the operation of the system. They played key roles in facilitating Epstein’s actions by providing the financial and legal support necessary for his sex-trafficking scheme. – The survivors in the lawsuit Indyke and Kahn deny knowing about or participating in Epstein’s crimes. Their attorneys said that no woman had accused the advisers of committing sexual abuse or directly witnessing it. Expenses are reducing the estate, but investments could increase what remains Since Epstein’s death, his estate has paid survivors nearly $170 million. A federal judge recently ordered an information campaign regarding a $35 million settlement and set a new 60-day deadline for filing compensation claims. Each year, the estate spends approximately $10–15 million on legal and other services. Those funds also cover Indyke’s and Kahn’s defense in civil cases in which they are accused of aiding Epstein’s crimes. At the same time, some investments could replenish the estate’s assets. In 2015–2016, Epstein invested $40 million in two funds operated by Valar Ventures, a company co-founded by Peter Thiel. According to Indyke’s testimony, those investments are now valued at approximately $172 million, and their term expires in 2026. Another fund, which is being prepared for liquidation, is valued at less than $10 million. The exact amount that can be recovered after the assets are sold is unknown. The estate’s remaining value could also be reduced by new lawsuits, taxes, and legal expenses. In December 2022, the estate agreed to pay the U.S. Virgin Islands $105 million in cash, half of the proceeds from the sale of Little Saint James, more than $80 million in tax benefits, and $450,000 in compensation for environmental damage. Who is supposed to receive money under Epstein’s will According to the will and documents related to the “1953 Trust,” released by the U.S. Department of Justice in January, Epstein’s partner, Karyna Shuliak, is first among the recipients. She was promised $50 million in cash and another $50 million in lifelong monthly payments. Darren Indyke was bequeathed $50 million, while Richard Kahn was bequeathed $25 million. Approximately 40 other recipients, including Epstein’s employees, friends, and their children, were to receive millions of dollars. Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s convicted accomplice, and his brother Mark Epstein were each allotted $10 million. However, the documents establish the order of payments: if funds are insufficient, the estate must first pay Shuliak, then Indyke and Kahn, and only afterward the other beneficiaries. Paying Shuliak, Indyke, and Kahn alone would require at least $175 million in cash. Therefore, it currently appears unlikely that Maxwell, Mark Epstein, and the other recipients will receive money. Indyke and Kahn have publicly stated that they do not expect to receive any payments until all legal proceedings are completed and the estate is settled. If and when Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn receive any funds from the “1953 Trust,” it will occur only after all claims against the estate have been finally resolved and the estate administration process has been completed. – A joint statement from the attorneys for Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn Jennifer Freeman, an attorney for the survivors, said that Indyke’s and Kahn’s positions could create a conflict of interest. They are simultaneously co-executors of the estate, defendants in lawsuits, and beneficiaries of the trust. The judge rejected that argument. A separate compensation program established after Epstein’s death paid approximately $125 million to 150 claimants. Participation was voluntary: people who accepted compensation waived future claims, while other survivors retained the right to go to court. What happens to the remaining funds will depend on new claims by survivors, the outcomes of the legal proceedings, tax obligations, and the amount that can be recovered from the sale of the investments. These factors will determine whether any money remains for the survivors and the trust’s beneficiaries. The Florida Department of Health confirmed on Sept. 18, 2026, that the death of an elderly woman on Sept. 4 was due to dengue fever. This is the first confirmed death in a larger dengue outbreak in Hillsborough County, which has seen 134 cases of the disease this summer. In August, the Hillsborough County Health Department issued a mosquito-borne illness alert due to reports of multiple locally acquired cases. This cluster of locally spread cases is a stark reminder that a disease which most Americans associate with faraway tropical vacations is increasingly being caught at home. Ad Feedback Dengue is often called “breakbone fever,” and the nickname is earned. People who get sick typically develop a sudden high fever along with a pounding headache, pain behind the eyes and deep aches in the muscles, joints and bones. Many also feel nauseated, throw up or break out in a blotchy rash a few days in. As an infectious diseases physician and tropical medicine specialist who directs a travel clinic, I see how easily dengue slips past both patients and doctors. In parts of the U.S. where the disease is still uncommon, it is easily mistaken for the flu or COVID-19, and that delay can be dangerous. Related article Northern house mosquito (Culex pipiens) with reflection on the blue water surface, macro shot with generous copy space, selected focus, narrow depth of field fermate/iStockphoto/Getty Images Mosquitoes bite! 5 tips for making yourself less attractive to them 5 min read How it spreads Dengue is not passed from person to person like a cold. It spreads through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti, a species commonly found in Florida. These mosquitoes thrive in warm cities and can breed in as little as a bottle capful of standing water. These mosquitoes bite during the day, not just at dusk. The cycle is simple and hard to break: A mosquito bites an infected person, then bites someone else days later, giving them the virus. Read more: We studied 3 Florida mosquito species to learn why they like some people more than others Dengue is especially tricky because most infections cause no symptoms at all. Roughly 3 in 4 people who catch the virus never feel sick. For the 25% who are symptomatic, those symptoms don’t appear until four to 10 days after being bitten. In addition, there are four different strains of the dengue virus, and surviving one gives you lasting protection against only that one. A second infection with a different type actually raises the odds of severe disease. A life-threatening turn Most people suffer with dengue for a miserable week and then recover on their own. But about 1 in 20 patients progress to severe dengue, a life-threatening turn that tends to strike just as the fever breaks – often around days three to seven, when patients and their families may wrongly assume the worst is over. In severe dengue, tiny blood vessels throughout the body start leaking fluid, blood pressure can crash and dangerous bleeding or organ damage can follow. Warning signs that someone is sliding into this phase include severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, extreme drowsiness or restlessness, and blood in vomit or stool. Some groups face higher risk, including infants, pregnant women, adults over 65 and people with conditions like diabetes, obesity or kidney disease. Left untreated, severe dengue can kill up to 10% of patients. With prompt hospital care, that number drops below 1 in 100 – which is why recognizing it early matters so much. A dengue vaccine exists, but it is not recommended for the average American traveler. The available shots are used only in select cases, such as children who live in high-transmission areas and have already had dengue once. So prevention still rests mostly on avoiding mosquito bites. Related article An adult female blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) is shown questing on a stick, 2023. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images The bugs are getting worse 11 min read How dengue is treated There is no antiviral drug that cures dengue. Care is all about supporting the body while it fights the virus. For people well enough to stay home, that means rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known in the U.S. by the brand name Tylenol, for fever and pain. Patients who may have dengue must avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. These drugs raise the risk of bleeding, which is already a danger with dengue. Read more: Dengue fever is a growing problem: why it’s so hard to beat with vaccines Patients who develop more severe symptoms need to be admitted to the hospital, where doctors give carefully measured intravenous fluids and watch closely. Too little fluid and the patient can go into shock; too much and the lungs can flood. A worsening global problem Dengue is surging worldwide. The World Health Organization recorded more than 14 million cases in 2024, its worst year on record, across some 100 countries. That’s a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases reported in 2000. Warmer temperatures, rapid urban growth and global travel are all helping the mosquitoes – and the virus – expand into places where it has never been a problem before. South Asia, Southeast Asia and Latin America carry the heaviest burden, but the map is spreading north. Related article Michelle Mingrone checks on mosquito traps in her yard in the morning of Monday, June 15, 2026, in Washington, DC. /Maansi Srivastava Why can’t we just get rid of mosquitoes? One fed-up community is trying 7 min read Why the U.S. should pay attention Most U.S. dengue cases are still picked up abroad. Travelers return home sick. In 2023 alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such travel-related cases. But every infected traveler is a spark, and in warm states the tinder is already there. In the U.S. territories, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands see the most cases by far. Florida has the highest risk among the 50 states, with Miami-Dade County recording more than 300 locally acquired dengue infections between 2010 and 2024. Local cases have also turned up in Texas, California, Arizona and Hawaii. Read more: How do mosquito repellents work? What to do if you think you have dengue If you develop a sudden fever after traveling to a dengue-prone area, or after mosquito exposure in South Florida, see a doctor and mention where you’ve been. Rest, drink fluids and use acetaminophen – not ibuprofen or aspirin. Most importantly, watch for the warning signs. Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or sudden drowsiness means get to an emergency room right away. And to protect yourself and your neighbors: Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and dump out any standing water in your yard where mosquitoes breed. supplementary_news.content_title: Three dengue fever cases in Orange, as state issues mosquito-illness warning
supplementary_news.content: Two more locally aquired cases of dengue fever in Orange County have prompted county officials to step up efforts to fight the pesky insects and the Florida Department of Health to issue an alert about mosquito-borne diseases. The first advisory about dengue fever was issued Sept. 2 by state officials after a case was confirmed in Pine Hills. The additional cases announced Friday are in the Apopka area and prompted another state alert. The culprits are Aedes aegypti, primarily daytime biters that thrive in urban and suburban areas and breed in flowerpots, buckets and other smaller containers, said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control. “We have a robust population of those,” he said of the species, sometimes called yellow fever mosquitos. “If residents go out in their yards and find containers holding water, more than likely there will be Aedes aegypti larvae in them.” Empty them, he advised. If larvae are in the containers, adult mosquitoes are around the property, too, Harrison said. The mosquitoes are homebodies, typically flying no more than 200 yards from where they emerged as larvae. Florida leads the nation in dengue cases this year with 270 reported so far. Specialist Jenifer Gonzalez studies dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Jonah Mock prepares samples to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Rafael Melendez, left, consults with lab manager Jose Colon while studying dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Jonah Mock holds a sample to be tested for dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialists Rafael Melendez, right, and Jenifer Gonzalez study dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Specialist Jonah Mock prepares samples to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Show Caption 1 of 6 Specialist Jenifer Gonzalez studies dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Expand Mosquito-borne dengue fever is commonly found in tropical and subtropical regions. Typical symptoms are a high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle, bone or joint pain, nausea and vomiting, swollen glands, and skin rash. While many species of mosquito inhabit Florida, only two transmit dengue: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Recognizable by their dark bodies and distinct white-striped legs, these biters peak just after sunrise and before sunset. They also can transmit Zika, yellow fever, and chikungunya . Aedes aegypti are native to north Africa and considered an invasive species here. A species collection displays the Aedes aegypti mosquito that is responsible for the dengue fever being tested by the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Last month, the Florida Department of Health in Orange County advised residents of an increase in mosquito-borne disease activity in the area. Several sentinel chickens have tested positive for West Nile virus. Sentinel chickens are healthy birds placed in outdoor coops and monitored by public health departments in the hopes of detecting potentially dangerous, mosquito-borne viruses before they spread to people. Though 2026 has been the 15th driest year in Central Florida since record-keeping began over a century ago, regular and sometimes heavy afternoon downpours this month have provided good conditions for Aedes aegypti. “Small containers — their breeding habitats — are filled nearly daily with rainwater, and that’s a problem,” Harrison said. He said mosquito control follows the guidance of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, focusing their initial response within about 200 yards of the area of concern. “Our crews inspect properties yard-to-yard for mosquito breeding sites, particularly containers and other sources of standing water where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can develop, and treat those sites as necessary,” he said. County crews also apply “larvicide treatments” using truck-mounted air-blast equipment. “These treatments are designed to reach water-holding containers and other mosquito-breeding habitats throughout the surrounding community and control mosquitoes while they are still in the larval stage,” Harrison said. Orange County Mosquito Control recently added new technology to its laboratory, allowing the agency to detect mosquito-borne illnesses, like dengue fever, more rapidly. The new molecular testing uses technology to look for genetic material of specific viruses within mosquito samples. Previously, samples were sent to outside laboratories. Specialist Rafael Melendez studies dead mosquitos to be tested for Dengue fever in the Orange County Mosquito Control lab in Orlando, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel) Harrison said the county can now get same-day results, which lead to faster responses and mitigation efforts. As many as 111 people as of early September have contracted locally acquired dengue in six Florida counties this year, according to state data. While eight of these cases were in Miami-Dade and Palm Beach counties, a striking 95 occurred in Hillsborough County, where mosquito control teams are working overtime and ramping up spraying. The death of an 80-year-old South Tampa woman may be linked to a dengue infection. Frequent global travel significantly drives case numbers. So far this year, about 160 Floridians contracted dengue after traveling to endemic areas — most frequently Cuba. Mosquito experts point to hotter summers and increased rainfall as additional contributing factors. A common dengue symptom is a sudden high fever starting four to 10 days after a bite, followed by a skin rash a few days later. Treatment is limited to rest, fluids, and pain relievers. “There is no cure or antiviral medications for dengue,” said Dr. Rana Chakraborty, division chief in Pediatric Infectious Diseases at the University of Miami. Many infected individuals remain completely unaware. “A lot of people can get bitten, acquire dengue, and nothing happens to them,” Chakraborty said. “Only a fraction have symptoms.” For about 1 in 20 people, dengue progresses to a severe level — triggering repeated vomiting, nosebleeds, stomach pain, and organ failure — often requiring hospitalization. shudak@orlandosentinel.com
