152 local cases in Florida By Josh Frigerio FOX 35 Orlando Orange County News Published September 18, 2026 12:51 PM EDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published September 18, 2026 12:51 PM EDT Orange County confirms 2 new locally acquired dengue cases Orange County health officials have confirmed two new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in Apopka, bringing the county's total to three cases and prompting a mosquito-borne illness alert. The Brief There have been 3 locally-acquired cases of dengue fever in Orange County, according to the Florida Department of Health. The two most recent cases were acquired in the Apopka area There have been more than 150 local cases of dengue reported in Florida, and 186 cases of international travel-related cases. ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. - There have been two more locally-acquired cases of dengue fever reported in Orange County, bringing the county total for the year to three, according to the Florida Department of Health and the Orange County Mosquito Control. County officials have now issued a mosquito alert and plan to target more areas with mosquito spray to reduce mosquito populations. New dengue cases reported in Orange County What we know: Officials said the two most recent cases were acquired in the Apopka area. What we don't know: Officials did not release specifics on the individuals who acquired the illness. More targeting mosquito spraying in Orange County What they're saying: "We are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in Pine Hills, Apopka, and throughout Orange County," said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control. "While CDC guidance calls for targeted treatment of areas of concern, we are taking additional measures. Given the increased Dengue Fever cases we are seeing in other parts of Florida, we want to be proactive to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." By the numbers: According to the Florida Department of Health's latest arbovirus surveillance weekly report, which runs Sept. 6-12: 41 new cases of locally-acquired dengue in Florida; 152 cases reported year to date 26 new cases of international travel-related cases of dengue; 186 cases reported year to date What is dengue? Dig deeper: Dengue is a virus spread through bites from two species of mosquitoes, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, according to Florida health officials. Both are found in Florida. When someone is infected, it can lead to dengue fever, a sometimes painful, debilitating disease. While rare, if symptoms are left untreated, it can be deadly. Dengue fever symptoms Symptoms typically appear 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, and usually last 4-7 days. Symptoms are similar to those of influenza and other viruses: Sudden fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain Bleeding Vomiting and diarrhea Can it be deadly? Dengue hemorrhagic fever, a more severe form of dengue, is rare, but can be deadly if not recognized and/or treated with supportive care, according to the Florida Department of Health's website. Treatment There is no treatment for dengue fever or dengue hemorrhagic fever. However, people should manage symptoms and complications. Tips for avoiding mosquito bites What you can do: There are a number of mosquito-borne illnesses found in Florida, including West Nile, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, as well as travel-related illnesses, like chikungunya fever, dengue fever, malaria, yellow fever, and Rift Valley fever. Health officials are urging residents to take steps to prevent mosquito bites: Use insect repellent on exposed skin or clothing Remove standing water to stop mosquitoes from breeding Keep doors, exterior windows closed The Source: This story uses information from news releases issued by both the Florida Department of Health in Orange County and Orange County Mosquito Control, as well as information on Dengue fever from DOH and the CDC. supplementary_news.content: India’s first approved dengue vaccine QDENGA likely to hit private market in 2027 QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries since 2022, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally, according to Takeda. South First Desk Published Sep 18, 2026 | 8:48 PM ⚊ Updated Sep 18, 2026 | 8:48 PM India’s dengue burden has been growing, with cases increasing 11-fold over the past two decades. Make Us Your Preferred Source on Google Synopsis: India’s first approved dengue vaccine, QDENGA, is expected to enter the private market in the first half of 2027, with Dr Reddy’s Laboratories handling its promotion and distribution in partnership with Takeda. The vaccine was approved by the CDSCO in July 2026 for people aged 4 to 60 and is given in two doses three months apart, with the company reporting efficacy against all four dengue virus serotypes. India’s first approved dengue vaccine is set to enter the country’s private market in 2027, with Hyderabad-based Dr Reddy’s Laboratories partnering with Japanese pharmaceutical company Takeda to promote and distribute its dengue vaccine QDENGA. It is expected to become available in the first half of 2027, subject to the completion of applicable regulatory processes. Dr Reddy’s will handle promotion and distribution in the private market, while Takeda will retain legal ownership and the rights to promote and distribute the vaccine in India’s public market. India’s dengue burden has been growing, with cases increasing 11-fold over the past two decades. A nationwide dengue surveillance study conducted by the Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory network of the Indian Council of Medical Research found that all four dengue virus serotypes, DENV-1 to DENV-4, are circulating across multiple regions of India. The study also found that around one in 14 patients had a concurrent infection with multiple dengue serotypes. Also Read: Emergency contraceptive pills may soon carry new warnings on packs in India Approved in 43 countries QDENGA became India’s first CDSCO-approved dengue vaccine after receiving marketing authorisation from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026 for individuals aged 4 to 60 years. Also known as TAK-003, it is a live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine designed to provide immune coverage against all four dengue virus serotypes. The vaccine is built on a DENV-2 backbone and contains structural proteins from DENV-1, DENV-3 and DENV-4. It is administered in two doses, three months apart. Takeda said its global clinical programme involved more than 60,000 participants across eight dengue-endemic countries. Its seven-year Phase 3 TIDES trial reported efficacy across all four dengue serotypes through seven years. QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries since 2022, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally, according to Takeda. The WHO has recommended the vaccine without pre-vaccination screening for use in high-endemic countries, and it has included the vaccine in its List of Prequalified Vaccines. (Edited by Dese Gowda with inputs from Sumit Jha)

from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) for people who are 4 to 60 years old. Kahekashan Created On: 18 Sept 2026 6:54 PM ISTComment Share : X India to Launch Qdenga the First Approved Dengue Vaccine in 2027 A− Font size A+ Select Hans India Now FOLLOW ON Google News Qdenga, Takeda’s dengue vaccine will be available in India in the half of 2027. Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories and Takeda Pharmaceutical Company announced on Friday, September 18 2026 that they have signed a distribution agreement. Under that agreement Dr. Reddy’s will distribute Qdenga in the Indian private market for children and adults. The companies said the vaccine will be available in the half of 2027 subject to the completion of relevant processes, with local authorities. Qdenga is the dengue vaccine that was approved in India. In July 2026 Qdenga got marketing approval from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation approved Qdenga for people who're 4 years old, to 60 years old. Although having it in India's public vaccination program is a goal for the future, it will be possible for some people to get the vaccine through the private market when it is available, said Takeda. The vaccine will be available, through Dr. Reddys. This will give people who're eligible a way to get the vaccine once it is ready. Also Read GCC intensifies anti-mosquito, dengue control operations Advertisement Discover more Book Walking Tours India News Portal Download Interactive Maps Through this partnership, Takeda and Dr. Reddy’s will work together to connect with doctors and increase knowledge about the disease. They will also help sell and get Qdenga into the private market for children and adults. They will do this while following all the rules that're in place now. "Our partnership with Dr. Reddy’s in the market will help people get Qdenga quickly when it is available in India, " said Dr. Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, for Takeda’s International Business Unit. He welcomed the recommendation from the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health to add a dengue vaccine to the Universal Immunization Programme. This recommendation shows that dengue is now seen as a public health challenge. "We believe that the introduction of the dengue vaccine approved in India represents a big step forward for the country’s healthcare. Through our partnership with Takeda we are excited to make Qdenga available to those who qualify and to help reduce the impact of dengue across the nation, " said MV Ramana, CEO of Dr. Reddy’s Global Generics division. Also Read Special measures to control communicable diseases amid rains Dr. Reddy’s will be the partner responsible for promoting and distributing the vaccine in the private market. This includes both adult vaccinations. Takeda keeps the rights to promote and distribute Qdenga in India’s market. Takeda also holds ownership of Qdenga. They have control over medical oversight and the overall branding of Qdenga, in the country. Qdenga (TAK-003) is a vaccine that has been made strong so it can help the body build protection. It is made from a DENV-2 type of virus. This vaccine includes parts from the DENV-1, DENV-3 and DENV-4 types of viruses. This helps the body fight all four types of dengue viruses. The vaccine is given in two shots. The time between the two shots is three months. Dengue still stands as a changing health problem in India. Dengue cases have grown eleven times in the twenty years. A big dengue watch study carried out by the Indian Council of Medical Research’s Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory shows that all four dengue virus types-DENV‐1, DENV‐2, DENV‐3 DENV‐4-are found at the time in many parts of the country. Dengue also shows that one in fourteen people has more than one dengue type at once according to the companies, in a joint statement. supplementary_news.content_title: Dr Reddy's, Takeda Ink Deal to Launch Dengue Vaccine QDENGA in India's Private Market in 2027
supplementary_news.content: Dr Reddy's, Takeda Ink Deal to Launch Dengue Vaccine QDENGA in India's Private Market in 2027 Hyderabad: Dr Reddy's Laboratories and Takeda Pharmaceutical Company have entered into an exclusive collaboration to promote and distribute QDENGA, Takeda's dengue vaccine, in India's private healthcare market. The partnership will cover both paediatric and adult vaccination. Subject to the completion of applicable processes with local authorities, the vaccine is expected to become available in India during the first half of 2027. QDENGA received marketing authorisation from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026 for use in individuals aged four to 60 years. According to the companies, it is the first dengue vaccine to receive approval in India. Under the agreement, Dr Reddy’s will be exclusively responsible for promoting, marketing and distributing QDENGA in India’s private market. Takeda will retain the rights to commercialise the vaccine in the country’s public market and will remain responsible for its manufacture and import. Takeda will also retain legal ownership of the vaccine and continue to oversee its medical, regulatory and brand strategy in India. The agreement does not involve any upfront consideration or milestone payments, while the remaining commercial terms have been kept confidential. The two companies will jointly support disease awareness, engagement with healthcare professionals and the private-market introduction of the vaccine in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements. Also Read: USFDA Issues Two Observations After Records Assessment of Dr. Reddy's Mexico API Facility The collaboration comes amid continuing concern over India’s dengue burden. According to information shared by the companies, reported dengue cases in the country have increased substantially over the past two decades. Surveillance findings have also shown that all four dengue virus serotypes—DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4—are circulating across multiple regions. M.V. Ramana, CEO, Global Generics, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories, described the approval of India’s first dengue vaccine as an important development for the country’s healthcare landscape. “Through our collaboration with Takeda, we look forward to making QDENGA available to eligible individuals and contributing to efforts aimed at addressing the country’s dengue burden,” he said. Dr Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, International Business Unit, Takeda, said the company remained committed to supporting India’s evolving healthcare needs and expanding access to dengue vaccination. He also referred to the Parliamentary Committee on Health’s recommendation that a dengue vaccine be considered for inclusion in the Universal Immunisation Programme. In the meantime, the partnership with Dr Reddy’s is expected to facilitate access through the private market once QDENGA becomes commercially available. QDENGA, also known as TAK-003, is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to provide protection against all four dengue virus serotypes. It is administered as a two-dose regimen, with the doses given three months apart. The vaccine has been evaluated through a global clinical programme involving more than 60,000 participants. This included the seven-year Phase III TIDES trial conducted across eight dengue-endemic countries. Since 2022, QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries, including India. More than 32 million doses have reportedly been distributed through public and private vaccination programmes worldwide. The vaccine has also been prequalified by the World Health Organization. Dr Reddy’s said the partnership supports its strategy to strengthen its vaccine business in India while contributing to wider public-health efforts aimed at reducing the country’s dengue burden. The Florida Department of Health says the mosquito-borne illness claimed the life of an elderly woman earlier this month. Advertisement Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Florida currently leads the nation in dengue fever cases, and experts are concerned because many of those infections have been acquired within the state. The CDC said Florida has seen more than 330 cases of dengue fever this year. The Florida Department of Health said 152 of those are locally acquired, with the current outbreak centered north of Tampa. Florida confirms a death from dengue as the state struggles with one of its worst recent outbreaks “We have not seen this for close to over 100 years, almost. And this is very concerning. It is very alarming, and we need to be very careful about how we approach this,” Dr. Moti Ramgopal, an infectious diseases specialist at Florida Coast Medical Center, said. Ramgopal said dengue is typically picked up by people who have traveled abroad to countries in the Caribbean or Latin America, and the effects range in severity. Dengue fever case confirmed in Palm Beach County “You can have the body aches within 2 to 3 days, flu-like symptoms, headaches. And those are your symptoms that you will say, well, I'm not feeling well, is this severe? And we call it dengue hemorrhagic fever because sometimes you can get bleeding from it,” Ramgopal said. Follow us on social: Facebook | X | Instagram | YouTube | TikTok Crews in the Tampa area are working to spray mosquitoes both day and night, but mosquito control in Palm Beach County is not following the same approach. “There's not currently any local dengue transmission in Palm Beach County. There was in August. There isn't any longer. We're just continuing operating. Business as usual. Treating as necessary,” Ryan Sullivan, with Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management, said. Dengue fever case in Palm Beach County prompts mosquito control action The agency is currently only conducting ground treatments and is standing by to determine if they need to add aerial spraying in the future. “We're continuing to actively monitor our surveillance trapping; the mosquito that vectors dengue is a container breeding mosquito called Aedes aegypti, or the yellow fever mosquito. The risk levels are low. We monitor for imported cases where patients have traveled. We work closely with the health department,” Sullivan said. In the meantime, experts are urging people to educate themselves about dengue and take precautions like wearing protective clothing, using bug sprays, and getting rid of potential mosquito breeding grounds like standing water in their communities. supplementary_news.content: The Chenab Times Tamil Nadu Records Significant Spike in Dengue Cases: New Figures Revealed News Desk CT 2 days ago Aedes mosquito and a colorized transmission electron micrograph of dengue virus particles (yellow/r... — NIAID / CC BY 2.0 Ad New figures released by the Tamil Nadu State Health Department indicate a substantial increase in dengue cases over the past three years, prompting renewed attention to public health monitoring and vector control measures. The Chenab Times has learned that the latest data reveals a stark upward trend, with reported cases significantly exceeding previous estimates. The department’s figures show 56,863 dengue cases in 2023, followed by 46,971 cases in 2024. Projections for 2025 indicate a continued high incidence, with 25,585 cases already reported. These numbers represent a considerable deviation from the corresponding figures that were previously made available by the National Centre for Vector Borne Disease Control (NCVBDC). The discrepancy suggests a potential underestimation of the dengue burden in the state by national surveillance systems or a recent acceleration in case detection and reporting by the state health authorities. Health officials are reportedly reviewing the methodologies and data collection processes to understand the reasons behind this divergence. Dengue fever, a mosquito-borne viral infection, poses a significant public health challenge globally, and particularly in tropical and subtropical regions like Tamil Nadu. The disease can range in severity from mild febrile illness to severe dengue, which can be fatal. Common symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, rash, and nausea. The alarming rise in dengue cases underscores the persistent threat of vector-borne diseases and the critical need for robust public health infrastructure and community engagement. Factors contributing to the spread of dengue often include inadequate sanitation, poor waste management leading to breeding sites for mosquitoes, and climatic conditions that favour mosquito proliferation. Health experts emphasize that proactive measures are crucial in combating dengue outbreaks. These include source reduction of mosquito breeding sites through environmental management, personal protection against mosquito bites, and prompt diagnosis and treatment of infected individuals. Public awareness campaigns play a vital role in educating communities about preventive strategies and recognizing early symptoms of the disease. In response to the escalating figures, state health authorities are expected to intensify their surveillance activities, enhance public awareness programs, and reinforce vector control operations across the state. This includes increased fogging, larvicidal treatments, and promoting community participation in eliminating mosquito breeding grounds in and around residential areas. The release of these revised figures is anticipated to spur further investigation into the epidemiological patterns of dengue in Tamil Nadu and potentially influence policy decisions related to disease prevention and control at both state and national levels. The focus remains on mitigating the impact of the disease and protecting public health. News Desk CT The Chenab Times News Desk Exit mobile version

supplementary_news.content: Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Hillsborough Dengue Cases Reach 134 as Florida Total Hits 152 By Rob Garguilo Sep 18, 2026 Photo: martinatobolova / iStock / Getty Images Hillsborough County, FL - Florida health officials reported another increase in locally acquired dengue infections, with Hillsborough County accounting for most of the state’s cases. The county has recorded 134 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, according to the latest Florida Department of Health arbovirus surveillance data. Florida’s statewide total has reached 152 cases. Locally acquired cases involve people infected by mosquitoes in Florida rather than during travel to another country or region where dengue circulates. Hillsborough previously reported 95 local infections through Sept. 5. The latest update added 39 cases to the county’s annual total. The infections have primarily involved dengue virus type 2, also known as DENV-2. State surveillance previously detected the same virus type in Aedes aegypti mosquito samples collected in Hillsborough County. Aedes aegypti mosquitoes commonly live near homes, bite during daylight hours and reproduce in containers holding standing water. Mosquitoes can acquire dengue by biting an infected person and later transmit the virus through additional bites. Dengue does not normally spread directly between people. Symptoms can include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, rash and muscle or joint pain. Most patients recover within about a week, but some develop severe dengue requiring immediate medical treatment. Warning signs may include intense abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, extreme fatigue, restlessness or difficulty breathing. Health officials recommend using insect repellent, wearing clothing that covers exposed skin, maintaining window and door screens, and removing standing water from buckets, flowerpots, tires, toys and other outdoor containers. Anyone experiencing possible dengue symptoms should contact a health care provider. Immediate treatment is recommended if severe warning signs develop. supplementary_news.content: Dengue, spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, remains a serious health threat. Early consultation and prevention are key. AI Text size BALER, Aurora — Dengue cases in Aurora surged 137 percent from the same period last year, reaching 2,172 cases from 4 January to 12 September 2026, with seven deaths recorded, according to the Provincial Health Office. Children ages 1 to 10 accounted for nearly half of all infections, with 917 cases, or 42 percent of the provincial total. During the latest surveillance week, from 6 to 12 September, the PHO recorded 106 new cases. Patients ranged in age from 1 month to 104 years, with a median age of 12. Males accounted for half of all reported cases. Maria Aurora recorded the highest cumulative number of infections with 463 cases, followed by Dilasag with 413 and Dingalan with 394. Among newly reported cases, San Luis recorded the most with 32, followed by Maria Aurora with 26 and Dilasag with 21. Baler logged 11 new infections for a total of 242 cases, while Casiguran recorded eight new cases for a total of 253. Dipaculao and Dinalungan each reported one new case, bringing their totals to 69 and 37, respectively. Dilasag posted the province’s highest attack rate at 23.2 cases per 1,000 population, indicating a more intense concentration of infections compared with other municipalities. The PHO also reported clustering of dengue cases in 61 barangays across Aurora, showing that transmission was not confined to a single municipality. Nationwide, the Department of Health recorded 155,918 dengue cases, down 33 percent from the same period last year. Central Luzon, which includes Aurora, had the highest number of cases among the country’s regions with 21,242, followed by Calabarzon and Metro Manila. Health authorities have warned that rainy conditions and flooding create additional breeding grounds for mosquitoes that transmit dengue. Dengue can become life-threatening if severe symptoms are not recognized and treated promptly. Symptoms may include fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, vomiting and rashes. Provincial health officials urged households to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, use protective measures such as mosquito nets and repellents, seek immediate medical consultation when symptoms develop and support targeted fogging in outbreak areas. “Dengue prevention is everyone’s responsibility. Act now, clean your surroundings, and help us stop this outbreak,” the PHO said. Authorities stressed that early detection and prompt medical attention remain critical in preventing severe dengue as rains continue across the province

supplementary_news.content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Entertainment Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Motor Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Florida is facing a severe dengue outbreak and has confirmed its first death of the year Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Monday, September 21, 2026 - 12:36 Aedes aegypti (Reference image)Photo © Wikimedia Commons Florida confirmed its first death from dengue in 2026 amid a rise in infections acquired within the state, with Hillsborough County in the Tampa area becoming the main hotspot of the outbreak. The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death on Friday, according to AP, while local reports indicated that the victim was an 80-year-old woman from Tampa who died on September 4. The confirmation comes when the official data itself shows an unusual expansion of transmission. The latest arbovirus surveillance report from the Florida Department of Health, corresponding to the week of September 6 to 12, recorded 152 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, spread across six counties. The vast majority are concentrated in Hillsborough, with 134 local infections, followed by Miami-Dade and Pinellas, with seven cases each; Pasco, with two; and Orange and Palm Beach, with one each in that official count. The growth has been particularly rapid in Hillsborough. On September 4, Florida's Surgeon General, Joseph Ladapo, officially reported 59 locally acquired infections in that county. Just over a week later, the state report recorded 134. Furthermore, the Orange County Health Department announced last Friday two additional local cases of dengue, subsequent to the period covered by the latest available weekly report, so the state count will continue to be adjusted as new reports come in. Florida is experiencing one of its most intense years of local transmission in recent times. According to the historical statistics from the Florida Department of Health, in 2023 the state recorded 199 locally acquired dengue cases, the highest number in the published series for the period 2014-2024. Dengue is a viral disease primarily transmitted through the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. It can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, headache, and skin rashes; in severe cases, it may lead to bleeding, shock, and even death. Authorities have intensified surveillance and mosquito control in the affected areas. The Department of Health recommends using repellents registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), wearing clothing that covers arms and legs when possible, and eliminating any standing water around homes and businesses, as even small amounts can become breeding grounds. The increase is not limited to Tampa Bay. Miami-Dade confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue in early August, while other counties were later added to the list of areas with local transmission. At the beginning of September, dengue cases were already showing a significant increase in Florida, with local transmission hotspots in various areas of the southern and central parts of the state. Health Dengue fever cases rise in Florida, with 3 new cases in Lee County and a death in Hillsborough County WGCU | By Cary Barbor, Jennifer Crawford Published September 21, 2026 at 10:26 AM EDT Facebook LinkedIn Email Print Three new cases of Dengue fever in Lee County and a death from the disease in Hillsborough County are part of the reported rise in cases of the mosquito-spread virus in Florida. Cases of the disease in the U.S. are typically picked up elsewhere in the world and brought home by travelers. That is the situation with the three cases in Lee County according to Jennifer McBride, Lee County Mosquito Control public information officer. McBride said those in Lee County who acquired the disease contracted it in Cuba and that there have been no locally-obtained dengue cases. "It starts with an international case," she said. "We have people travel somewhere, they've been bitten by a mosquito that's infected with dengue. They come back. The thing about dengue is about 80% of patients actually are asymptomatic. They don't have symptoms, which could be a problem. So they come back to here and a mosquito will bite them. It becomes infected with the dengue and then it will bite someone that has not traveled and it becomes localized. And very quickly then that takes off. So those mosquitoes are then transmitting a local case of dengue." Support for WGCU Provided By: U.S. Centers for Disease Control In the United States, there have been nearly 1,500 locally acquired U.S. cases, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Florida’s largest number — nearly 200 — was reported in 2023. This year, Florida alone reported 152 locally acquired cases of the disease, meaning it was spread by mosquito bites in the state. 134 of the cases are in Hillsborough County. Dengue can cause a high fever, joint pain and headache. The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes day and night. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed, said Paolo Pecora, senior environmental scientist for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services. The CDC shows that more than 330 cases have been reported in Florida in 2026 with eight cases in Lee County. McBride said that many of the cases reported in Hillsborough have also been linked to being acquired in Cuba. For now, McBride said, Lee County Mosquito Control personnel have been going door-to-door in Lee County requesting access to backyards and other areas to look for possible breeding sites for mosquitoes such as standing water in containers. The type of mosquito linked to the dengue cases is what's identified as the "backyard mosquito" also known as aedes aegypti. Another viral disease spread by mosquitoes is chikungunya. In the week ended September 12, eight new cases were reported in Miami-Dade county. This illness also is characterized by a high fever and joint pain. Support for WGCU Provided By: The best way to avoid transmission is to avoid mosquito bites. Drain standing water from around your home, wear long sleeves and pants outdoors when possible, and protect yourself with mosquito repellant. Dengue at a glance/CDC data All four dengue viruses are spread to people primarily through the bite of an infected Aedes species mosquito. Protect yourself from dengue by avoiding mosquito bites. There are no dengue vaccines currently available in the United States. Prevention The best way to prevent dengue is to protect yourself from mosquito bites. Use insect repellent. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. Take steps to control mosquitoes in and around your home. If you think you have dengue See a healthcare provider if you develop a fever or have symptoms of dengue. Tell him or her about any recent travel. Rest as much as possible. Take acetaminophen (also known as paracetamol outside of the US) to control fever and relieve pain — Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen! Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated. Drink water or drinks with added electrolytes. For mild symptoms, care for a sick infant, child, or family member at home. Important tip If you have dengue, prevent mosquito bites. During the first week of illness, dengue can be found in the blood. The virus can be passed from an infected person to a mosquito through mosquito bites. WGCU is your trusted source for news and information in Southwest Florida. We are a nonprofit public service, and your support is more critical than ever. Keep public media strong and donate now. Thank you. The Associated Press contributed to this report. FOX 35 Orlando Gainesville News - FOX 51 Gainesville Atlanta News - FOX 5 Atlanta About Us Meet the FOX 13 team TV Listings Jobs & Internships WTVT History Closed Captioning FCC Public File FCC Applications Contact Us FOX Tampa Bay Live Stream live Interviews & segments Stream on FOX One NFL Live Streaming College Football Live Streaming MLB Live Streaming NASCAR Live Stream IndyCar Live Streaming Men's College Basketball Live Stream Women's College Basketball Live Stream WNBA Live Stream MLS Live Stream River Flood Warning is in effect, Citrus County 2 Marine Weather Statement until WED 7:00 PM EDT, Coastal waters from Englewood to Tarpon Springs FL out 20 NM Dengue fever-related death reported in Hillsborough as mosquito treatments continue By Ariel Plasencia FOX 13 News Hillsborough County Updated September 18, 2026 5:57 PM EDT Published September 18, 2026 5:18 PM EDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Updated September 18, 2026 5:57 PM EDT ▾ Dengue cases surge to 134, first death confirmed 0:00 3:01 ▶ Dengue cases surge to 134, first death confirmed More than 130 cases of dengue have been reported in Hillsborough County, making up 88% of the state’s total infections, according to most recent data from Florida health officials. FOX 13's Ariel Plasencia reports. The Brief Hillsborough County now accounts for 88% of Florida’s locally acquired dengue cases, with 134 infections reported so far, according to recent state health data. Doctors with Tampa General Hospital estimate they’ve treated over 100 dengue patients, and symptoms include a "break-bone fever." Mosquito control crews are deploying helicopters and trucks in an aggressive campaign to kill mosquito larvae, as well as adult mosquitos. TAMPA, Fla. - More than 130 cases of dengue have been reported in Hillsborough County, making up 88% of the state’s total infections, according to most recent data from Florida health officials. Of those, the Florida Department of Health also confirmed the first dengue fever-related death in the county. The numbers show 39 cases of dengue were reported in Hillsborough County from Sept. 6-12 alone. Meanwhile, seven total cases have been reported in Pinellas County and Pasco County has two cases. The treatment plan Local perspective: Crews with Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services will continue to use helicopters and trucks to spray treatment, aimed at killing both adult mosquitos and mosquito larvae. County officials told FOX 13 they believe these efforts appear to be working because mosquito trap numbers are dropping in certain locations. Additionally, samples of adult mosquitos from local traps have come back negative for dengue over the last two weeks. Furthermore, laboratory testing confirms that potentially infected female mosquitoes are not passing the virus down to their offspring, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management officials said. "It makes me feel good. Again, it's a suppression and eradication campaign," Paolo Pecora, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management senior environmental scientist, told FOX 13. "We want to go into there and make sure that we are eliminating any flying disease vector that can potentially transmit this virus to our residents." Why you should care: But, they aren’t letting their guard down. County officials don’t want mosquitos that have already bitten somebody with dengue to go and bite somebody else, resulting in more human cases. So, they’re asking for the public’s help. "This mosquito species is strictly containers. Not ditches, not sewer drainage areas, not lakes and ponds. It's containers," said Pecora. "They are utilizing and have evolved with mankind through civilizations to utilize man-made objects. That’s why this is such a challenge and why we’re asking our residents to come out and help us." What you can do: Residents are urged to dump any standing water on their property and to wear bug spray when spending time outdoors. Local doctors treating dengue What they're saying: Doctors with Tampa General Hospital estimate they’ve treated more than 100 dengue patients, telling FOX 13 one of the common symptoms is a "break-bone fever." "The body aches are so intense that it's got this nickname as 'break-bone fever,'" said Dr. Kartik Cherabuddi, the chief hospital epidemiology officer at Tampa General Hospital. "It's real, and I've seen patients — they hurt so bad, it's the predominant thing that’s bringing them into the emergency room." Along with severe joint, bone, and muscle pain, common symptoms include nausea and pain behind the eyes. "It's the time the fever breaks. The next two days is when you can have more severe warning signs. If you have severe abdominal pain, persistently throwing up, bleeding from the gums or other sites, difficulty breathing — and critically, that’s when the fever starts to go down is when these could develop," Cherabuddi added. "That's when you absolutely have to go to the ER." He said one in four who are infected will develop the illness — and roughly one in 20 symptomatic people developed more severe disease. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from the Florida Department of Health, who provided recent infection data, as well as officials from Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services and doctors at Tampa General Hospital. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue hotspot map, where other mosquito-borne infections are C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 18, 2026, 12:59 p.m. ET Florida is experiencing a surge in locally acquired dengue fever cases, with 152 reported as of mid-September. The vast majority of cases, 134 in total, have been confirmed in Hillsborough County. Dengue is a mosquito-borne illness with symptoms including fever, severe pain, and rash. Florida is experiencing a surge in dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness that causes aches, pains, nausea, vomiting, and rash, according to state health data. The state reported 41 new locally acquired cases — meaning that people caught it in Florida, not while traveling abroad — in just the last week, bring the state total to 152 as of Sept. 12. Last year, 62 people tested positive. Nearly all of the cases have been reported in one area: Hillsborough County, home of Tampa, which has reported 134 confirmed locally acquired cases. The other 18 cases have been reported in Miami-Dade, Pinellas, Pasco, Orange, and Palm Beach counties. There have also been 186 dengue cases acquired this year from international travel. Shop mosquito repellent at Amazon Currently, 11 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites. Other mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida Health officials track several different endemic mosquito-borne viruses such as West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), St. Louis encephalitis virus, chikungunya virus, Zika virus (ZIKV), malaria, and California encephalitis group viruses. As of Sept. 12, five cases of West Nile virus have been reported in Florida, two of them asymptomatic, although the illness has been rapidly rising on the U.S. West Coast. One case of locally acquired and 66 cases of travel-based chikungunya fever also have been reported. Where has dengue been reported in Florida? According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 17, there have been 152 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported, which is up from 111 reported on Sept. 5. Hillsborough County: 134 (which jumped from 95 the week before) Miami-Dade County: 7 Pinellas County: 7 Pasco County: 2 Orange County: 1 Palm Beach County: 1 What is dengue fever? What are the symptoms? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include a sudden onset of fever, severe headaches, eye pain, muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”), bleeding, and in some cases, gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes that bite people who have the virus and spread it to others. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue can be caused by one of four related viruses: dengue virus 1, 2, 3, and 4. The bulk of the detected cases in Florida have been DENV-2. What is Florida doing to prevent dengue infections? The Florida Department Health has advised residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. “Use insect repellent, cover up when possible, and remove standing water around your home. Individual prevention helps protect you and your community,” State Surgeon General Dr. Joseph A. Ladapo said in a release. Affected counties have increased mosquito spraying and tested for dengue in mosquito pools to track the spread. So far, 16 DENV-2-infected mosquito pools have been found in Hillsborough County, according to health department data. How to avoid dengue fever The best way is to avoid getting bitten by mosquitos, especially if you live in an area under a mosquito alert or advisory. According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C. A. supplementary_news.content_title: Florida confirms a death from dengue amid outbreak
supplementary_news.content: Florida is experiencing one of its worst surges of dengue fever in decades, and the toll now includes a death. The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death Friday, though it didn't provide further details. It's one of more than 130 locally acquired dengue cases reported so far this year in Hillsborough County, which typically sees only a handful. (MORE: 'Mosquito disease days' for West Nile transmission becoming more frequent in US ) "This is wildly unusual for us," said Chris Wilkerson, a spokesperson for the county. The Tampa Bay Times first reported the death, described as an elderly Tampa woman who died Sept. 4. The current Florida outbreak of dengue is likely due to recent weather conditions that allowed the virus-spreading mosquitoes to multiply. For decades in the U.S., most reported dengue cases were in travelers infected in other countries, along with locally acquired cases in Puerto Rico. But in 2009-2010, Key West , Florida, reported the first dengue cases acquired in the continental U.S. outside of the Texas-Mexico border since 1945. The state's largest number — nearly 200 — was reported in 2023. But this year's total so far already ranks second, with 152 cases of locally acquired dengue cases so far, according to the Florida Department of Health. Many infected people don't get sick, meaning the number of cases reported in an outbreak can be an undercount of the real number of infections. But some experience headache, fever and flu-like symptoms. Severe cases can cause serious bleeding, shock and death. Across the world , more than 2.2 million infections have been reported so far this year, according to the World Health Organization, and nearly 1,200 have died. In the United States, there have been nearly 1,500 locally acquired U.S. cases, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . (MORE: Google wants to release 32 million mosquitoes in the US ) The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes day and night. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed, said Paolo Pecora, senior environmental scientist for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services. Recent sampling of mosquitoes has not been finding the virus, a sign that the likelihood of new infections is waning, Pecora said. Outbreaks can start when a person travels, gets infected and then is bitten back in the U.S. by a mosquito capable of spreading the virus. It can mushroom from there, said Michael von Fricken, a University of Florida associate professor of environmental and global health. Given the recurring abundance of those kinds of mosquitoes in Florida, the threat of dengue is not likely to tail off, he added. "I do think it's going to be somewhat the new normal," he said. supplementary_news.content_title: Gulfport town hall tackles dengue concerns and misinformation
supplementary_news.content: Gulfport leaders brought residents and mosquito-control officials together Monday night to answer questions about dengue as locally acquired cases continue to be reported across Tampa Bay. Vice Mayor Marlene Shaw said she organized the town hall after hearing misinformation and concerns about the virus and Pinellas County's mosquito-control response. "There has been so much conversation going on. I refer to it as chatter because a lot of it is misinformed information," Shaw said. "They're just going off in all different directions rather than going right to the facts." Shaw said she also had questions about mosquito-control treatments, including whether they could affect pollinators or be applied on private property. "There were so many reasons that even I was concerned," she said. Pinellas County is using Bti, or Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis , to target mosquito larvae in standing water before they develop into biting adults. The naturally occurring soil bacterium produces toxins that target the larvae of mosquitoes, blackflies and fungus gnats, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA says Bti does not pose a risk to people. Caroline Pickart, a senior environmental specialist with Pinellas County Mosquito Control, also addressed misconceptions about when dengue-carrying mosquitoes are active. The two primary mosquito species capable of spreading dengue, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , are daytime biters. An infected mosquito can transmit the virus through a single bite. "If a mosquito is infected with dengue, it does have the ability to pass that on to us when it bites us," Pickart said. "And that's through the ability of when they are biting us, they actually spit inside of us." Florida Department of Health data show 152 locally acquired dengue cases statewide through Sept. 12. That includes 134 cases linked to exposure in Hillsborough County, seven in Pinellas County and two in Pasco County. The report lists cases by the likely county of exposure, which may differ from where a patient lives. Hillsborough County accounts for nearly nine out of every 10 locally acquired cases reported in Florida during 2026. State health officials also reported cases in Miami-Dade, Orange and Palm Beach counties. "In Pinellas County, this is the first time we've seen a local dengue case in many years," Pickart said. Most people infected with dengue experience no symptoms or recover within about a week. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says approximately one in 20 people who become sick develop severe dengue, which can cause internal bleeding, shock or death. Warning signs can emerge within 24 to 48 hours after a fever goes away and may include abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or extreme fatigue and restlessness. Resident April Thanas said the meeting corrected advice she had considered sharing with her neighbors about creating a bucket containing a mosquito-control dunk. "I was going to start telling people to do that, so now I've learned not to do that," Thanas said. Shaw said she plans to share information from the meeting through local publications, while residents said they would pass what they learned to neighbors by word of mouth. The Tampa Bay Times first reported the death, described as an elderly Tampa woman who died Sept. 4. Dengue is caused by a virus spread by a type of warm weather mosquito that is expanding its geographic reach because of climate change, experts say. The current Florida outbreak is likely due to recent weather conditions that allowed the virus-spreading mosquitoes to multiply. For decades in the U.S., most reported dengue cases were in travelers infected in other countries, along with locally acquired cases in Puerto Rico. But in 2009-2010, Key West, Florida, reported the first dengue cases acquired in the continental U.S. outside of the Texas-Mexico border since 1945. The state's largest number — nearly 200 — was reported in 2023. But this year’s total so far already ranks second, with 152 cases of locally acquired dengue cases so far, according to the Florida Department of Health. Many infected people don’t get sick, meaning the number of cases reported in an outbreak can be an undercount of the real number of infections. But some experience headache, fever and flu-like symptoms. Severe cases can cause serious bleeding, shock and death. Across the world, more than 2.2 million infections have been reported so far this year, according to the World Health Organization, and nearly 1,200 have died. The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes day and night. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed, said Paolo Pecora, senior environmental scientist for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services. Recent sampling of mosquitoes has not been finding the virus, a sign that the likelihood of new infections is waning, Pecora said. Outbreaks can start when a person travels, gets infected and then is bitten back in the U.S. by a mosquito capable of spreading the virus. It can mushroom from there, said Michael von Fricken, a University of Florida associate professor of environmental and global health. Given the recurring abundance of those kinds of mosquitoes in Florida, the threat of dengue is not likely to tail off, he added. “I do think it’s going to be somewhat the new normal,” he said. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. Check your county's risk State sees 145% increase in dengue cases from last year C. A. Bridges Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Sept. 21, 2026, 2:11 p.m. ET Florida has reported its first dengue fever death of 2026 amid a surge in mosquito-borne illnesses. The death occurred in Hillsborough County, the hotspot for locally acquired cases in the state. State officials have reported 338 total dengue cases this year, with 152 acquired locally. Florida has reported the first dengue fever death of 2026 as cases of mosquito-borne illnesses surge in the state. The death occurred in Hillsborough County, the hotspot of this year's dengue cases, according to a statement from the Florida Department of Health shared with USA TODAY on Friday, Sept. 18. "We are reminding all residents and visitors throughout the state to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying insect repellent, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, draining any standing water, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible – especially during sunrise and sunset, when mosquitoes are most active," spokesperson Claire Maher said in a statement. The Tampa Bay Times was the first to report on the death, which it says occurred at Tampa General Hospital. The victim was 80-year-old Gay Small, the outlet reported. She died of “dengue infection” along with “septic shock” and “multi-organ failure," according to a death certificate obtained by the Times. How many 2026 dengue cases in Florida Florida officials have reported 338 cases of dengue fever this year as of Sept. 12, with 152 case acquired within the state and the rest from international travel. Of those local cases, 134 were reported in Hillsborough County. The other 18 cases have been reported in Miami-Dade, Pinellas, Pasco, Orange, and Palm Beach counties. That's a 145% increase in locally acquired cases over 2025, which saw 62. As of Sept. 17, 11 counties were under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. What is dengue fever? What are the symptoms? According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, dengue symptoms are very flu-like and include aches and pains, nausea, vomiting, and rash. About 1 in 20 people who contract dengue develop a more serious illness called hemorrhagic fever, which can bring symptoms like abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, and blood in stool or vomit. "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito. Where has dengue been reported in Florida? According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 17, Florida had reported 152 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 111 reported on Sept. 5. Hillsborough County: 134 (which jumped from 95 the week before) Miami-Dade County: 7 Pinellas County: 7 Pasco County: 2 Orange County: 1 Palm Beach County: 1 Which Florida counties are at risk for dengue fever? A mosquito-borne illness advisory (meaning residents should avoid mosquito bites) has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Brevard Leon Orange Palm Beach Pasco Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert (meaning there has been a rise in disease activity and residents should take extra precautions) has been issued for the following counties: Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Pinellas What is Florida doing to prevent dengue infections? The Florida Department of Health has advised residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. “Use insect repellent, cover up when possible, and remove standing water around your home. Individual prevention helps protect you and your community,” State Surgeon General Dr. Joseph A. Ladapo said in a release. Affected counties have increased mosquito spraying. So far, health department data show 16 DENV-2-infected mosquito pools in Hillsborough County. How to avoid dengue fever The best way is to avoid mosquito bites, especially if you live in an area under a mosquito alert or advisory. According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C. A.
